paper_title: SpecKCast: Spectral Kalman Forecasting for Diffusion Acceleration

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity image and video generation, but they suffer from substantial inference costs due to repeated transformer evaluations across many denoising steps. Feature caching reduces this cost by reusing features across denoising steps. Recent forecasting methods extend this idea by extrapolating features to skipped steps instead of reusing them. However, existing forecasting methods extrapolate the features they predict uniformly, even though the spatial-frequency components of these features change most at different stages of denoising. They also overlook that denoising progresses nonuniformly, so equal step intervals can correspond to very different amounts of change. These mismatches amplify forecast errors as more steps are skipped, limiting the achievable acceleration. We propose SpecKCast, a training-free method that forecasts the model output in the frequency domain. SpecKCast applies a 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT) to the output and tracks each coefficient with a lightweight Kalman filter along a band-specific time coordinate derived from the noise schedule. The filter tracks each coefficient's value and rate of change, and the transformer is evaluated only when the filter's forecast uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Wan2.1-14B, and HunyuanVideo show that SpecKCast achieves a better trade-off between acceleration and fidelity than existing caching and forecasting methods, reaching up to 6x speedup with less than 0.05 GiB of additional memory.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020) have become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity visual generation, gaining significant attention from recent advances in image and video generation. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) (Peebles & Xie, 2023) further improved generation quality by enabling greater model capacity. However, their costly forward passes throughout many denoising steps lead to substantially higher inference latency, limiting their use in real-time applications. To address this bottleneck, wide range of acceleration techniques have been proposed to reduce either the step count or the per-step cost, including efficient attention (Xia et al., 2025), step distillation (Salimans & Ho, 2022), and quantization (Li et al., 2023). Among these, feature caching has emerged as practical, training-free approach. Motivated by the observation that model outputs are highly similar across adjacent timesteps, these methods cache features from previous steps and reuse them in subsequent ones, skipping substantial computation (Ma et al., 2024; Selvaraju et al., 2024). However, this similarity decays as the gap between timesteps grows, so naive reuse over longer spans significantly degrades generation quality, limiting caching to modest acceleration ratios. To address this, recent work shifts from reusing features to forecasting them (Liu et al., 2025b; Han et al., 2026). Rather than assuming that cached feature remains valid at later timestep, forecasting methods exploit temporal continuity along the denoising trajectory, using features from previous steps to estimate their evolution and extrapolate their values at the target timestep. By modeling temporal drift, forecasting remains effective across wider timestep gaps, enabling higher acceleration ratios at comparable generation quality. Despite their promise, existing forecasting approaches impose uniformity on both what they forecast and how they model the signal over time (Liu et al., 2025b; Han et al., 2026). First, they extrapolate the model output or feature representation as whole, or apply the same forecasting rule uniformly to all of its components (e.g., channels), even though the spatial-frequency components of the signal evolve very differently. As Figure 2 shows, low-frequency content changes sharply in the first few steps and then settles, while high-frequency content changes slightly at first but evolves rapidly toward the end. Because these bands are active at different stages, single uniform forecaster may not serve them all. Second, existing methods use the samplers step index or raw diffusion timestep as their temporal coordinate, even though the amount of denoising performed at each step is nonuniform and depends on the scheduler. Therefore, equal intervals in the chosen coordinate can represent very different amounts of denoising progress. Treating these intervals as equivalent makes the resulting trajectory harder to model and forecast. Together, these limitations restrict achievable acceleration, amplify forecast errors, and degrade generation quality as the skip length increases. Motivated by this insight, we propose SpecKCast, training-free method that rethinks both what we forecast and how we extrapolate. The key idea is to forecast the models temporal evolution separately in the frequency domain, rather than uniformly in feature or latent space. SpecKCast transforms the model output into the spatial-frequency domain with 2D discrete cosine transform (DCT), and forecasts each coefficient during denoising. Moreover, instead of indexing the trajectory by the samplers timestep, SpecKCast exploits time coordinate derived from the noise scheduler and applies nonlinear time warping that improves the accuracy of local extrapolation within each band. To track each coefficient as it moves along its trajectory, SpecKCast uses lightweight Kalman filter, recursive state-space estimator that maintains the coefficients value and rate of change, projecting this state across skip and correcting it after full denoising step. The filter also estimates the uncertainty of each forecast. As more steps are skipped, this uncertainty increases, while the rate of change decays to keep the prediction stable. Furthermore, SpecKCast partitions the coefficients into frequency bands that share common temporal coordinate and forecast uncertainty, while each coefficient keeps its own value and rate of change. Finally, at skipped steps, the predicted coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain and passed directly to the sampler. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. Frequency-Decoupled and Scheduler-Aligned Forecasting. We introduce SpecKCast, training-free method that decomposes the model output in the spatial-frequency domain and forecasts its components along nonlinear time coordinate derived from the noise scheduler. Uncertainty-Aware Kalman Forecasting. SpecKCast uses lightweight Kalman filter to track frequency coefficient trajectories and leverage forecast uncertainty to maintain stability over skipped denoising steps. 2 Preprint. Under review. 2 RELATED WORK
Diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020) have become a leading approach for image and video generation.
Since the introduction of the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) (Peebles & Xie, 2023), many works have
built on this architecture, achieving strong results across diverse domains (Chen et al., 2024a; Yang
et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Rajabi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). This progress, however,
comes at a cost. Sampling requires many sequential forward passes through a large network, making
inference slow and expensive. This limits practical applications and has made diffusion model
acceleration an important research direction. A large body of work has therefore focused on reducing
sampling steps, mostly by distilling a multi-step teacher into a few-step student (Meng et al., 2023).
Examples include consistency models (Song & Dhariwal, 2024; Song et al., 2023) and DMD (Yin
et al., 2024a;b). Although effective, these approaches require additional training and are prone to
reduced sample diversity.
sections.content: A more recent line of work explores feature caching, which accelerates inference without any additional training. The core idea is to reuse intermediate features across timesteps to avoid redundant computation (Zou et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026). Early methods such as DeepCache (Ma et al., 2024) accelerated the U-Net backbone using handcrafted caching rules, and -DiT (Chen et al., 2024b) later extended this idea to DiT architectures. Subsequent methods further refine what and when to cache. FORA (Selvaraju et al., 2024) reuses attention and MLP outputs across timesteps, while TeaCache (Liu et al., 2025a) exploits the correlation between timestep embeddings and model outputs to estimate how much the output changes between steps and decide when to reuse cached features. HiCache (Feng et al., 2026) forecasts features with scaled Hermite polynomials to capture their non-monotonic dynamics in DiTs. SeaCache (Chung et al., 2026) instead improves the caching decision by measuring feature changes after spectral filter that preserves content-relevant components and suppresses noise. However, feature similarity decreases as the timestep gap increases. As more steps are skipped, the cached features deviate further from the actual ones, and these errors accumulate during sampling. This causes the trajectory to drift and degrades generation quality, limiting the achievable speedup. To address this, recent work shifts from reusing features to forecasting them (Liu et al., 2025b; Han et al., 2026). Instead of assuming that cached features remain valid at later timesteps, forecasting methods use features from previous steps to predict how they evolve and estimate their values at the target timestep. TaylorSeer (Liu et al., 2025b) does this locally with Taylor expansion, using finite differences of the most recent cached features, while Spectrum (Han et al., 2026) fits Chebyshev expansion over the full feature history to better capture long-range dynamics. By model3 Preprint. Under review. ing how features evolve, these methods remain effective over wider timestep gaps, enabling higher acceleration at comparable quality. However, both forecast uniformly in feature space and along the samplers timestep, ignoring that denoising progress is nonuniform across steps. In contrast, SpecKCast forecasts each frequency band separately along scheduler-derived time axis, using lightweight Kalman filter that adapts its forecasts as the trajectory evolves.

sections.title: 4 METHOD
sections.content: Spectral Kalman ForeCasting (SpecKCast) is an inference-time acceleration method for DiTs that reduces transformer evaluations during denoising. Unlike feature-caching methods that approximate an intermediate activation and still execute the remaining network layers, SpecKCast models the final velocity consumed by the sampler. SpecKCast applies 2D DCT to the model output and forecasts each frequency coefficient individually, while partitioning coefficients into bands that share forecast uncertainty and noise-schedule-derived time coordinate, warped nonlinearly to better align with each bands temporal evolution. SpecKCast uses Kalman filter to track each DCT coefficients value and temporal derivative, while sharing covariance statistics within each frequency band. The predicted coefficients are transformed back to the spatial domain and passed directly to the sampler.

sections.title: 4.1.1 SPATIAL-FREQUENCY DECOMPOSITION
sections.content: Forecasting the entire transformer output with single temporal model ignores an important property of diffusion predictions: different spatial frequencies exhibit different temporal dynamics, as shown in Figure 2. Low-frequency content settles early and drifts slowly, while high-frequency content remains active until the end of sampling. To account for these distinct dynamics, SpecKCast transforms each output into the spatial-frequency domain and forecasts its coefficients separately. Given the denoiser output Yj RCHW at timestep j, we apply an orthonormal 2D DCT independently to each channel, Zj = DCT2D(Yj), and partition the frequency plane into non-overlapping radial bands. Each frequency coefficient is treated as separate temporal signal and forecast by its own predictor, while the band determines how each coefficients dynamics are modeled. On steps where the transformer computes the full denoising step, the observed Zj updates the predictors; on skipped steps, the forecasters extrapolate each coefficients trajectory and together form (cid:98)Zj. sections.content: Setup. We evaluate SpecKCast on two state-of-the-art text-to-image models, FLUX.1-dev (Labs, 2024) at 1024 1024 and Qwen-Image (Wu et al., 2025) at 1328 1328, and further on two textto-video models, Wan2.1-14B (Wan et al., 2025) and HunyuanVideo (Kong et al., 2024). Following common practice, we use 50-step sampling as the full-computation reference for all models. We compare against FORA (Selvaraju et al., 2024), TeaCache (Liu et al., 2025a), HiCache (Feng et al., 2026), SeaCache (Chung et al., 2026), TaylorSeer (Liu et al., 2025b), and Spectrum (Han et al., 2026). Among them, TaylorSeer and Spectrum are the most closely related to our method, as they also forecast future features across timesteps instead of directly reusing cached ones. All baselines are evaluated using their official implementations. We decompose each prediction into = 7 frequency bands and, unless otherwise stated, set τ = 0.1, Tw = 2.0, and β = 0.6. For models that use classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022), SpecKCast forecasts the guided velocity (Section E). All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. 6 Preprint. Under review. Evaluation. For text-to-image generation, we use the DrawBench (Saharia et al., 2022) prompts and report ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023) and CLIP Score (Hessel et al., 2021), which measures textimage alignment. For text-to-video generation, we follow the standard prompts and protocol of VBench (Huang et al., 2024) and report its Quality Score, which aggregates dimensions such as temporal consistency, motion smoothness, and per-frame aesthetic and imaging quality. Since an accelerated sampler should reproduce the output of the full model rather than merely produce plausible sample, we also compare each accelerated sample with its 50-step reference generated from the same prompt and seed. We report PSNR for pixel-level error, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) for structural similarity, and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) for perceptual distance. For efficiency, we report sampling latency, speedup over the 50-step reference, and memory overhead (Mem. ), defined as the peak allocated GPU memory above that of Base at the same NFE. 5.1 TEXT-TO-IMAGE GENERATION Table 1 reports results on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image, where Base runs the original sampler with fewer steps to match the NFE. SpecKCast achieves the highest speedup among acceleration methods in all but one setting, along with the best PSNR and LPIPS in all settings and the best SSIM in all but one. At the highest acceleration, it outperforms the strongest baseline by 1.1 dB PSNR on FLUX.1dev (5.54) and 2.0 dB on Qwen-Image (6.00). Spectrum, the closest competitor at 14 and 10 NFE, trails SpecKCast by 0.51.4 dB PSNR and degrades sharply on Qwen-Image at 8 NFE, where its LPIPS rises to 0.527 compared with 0.267 for SpecKCast. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented SpecKCast, training-free method for accelerating Diffusion Transformers by forecasting the denoiser output at skipped sampling steps. Rather than modeling the output uniformly, SpecKCast decomposes it into spatial-frequency components and forecasts their distinct temporal dynamics along band-specific, noise-schedule-aligned time coordinates. lightweight Kalman filter tracks the value and rate of change of each DCT coefficient, while its uncertainty provides principled signal for adaptively determining when full transformer evaluation is needed. Across image and video diffusion models, SpecKCast consistently improves the accelerationquality tradeoff over existing caching and forecasting methods, achieving the best fidelity to the 50-step reference in most settings with negligible latency and memory overhead. These results highlight the benefit of explicitly accounting for the distinct temporal evolution of frequency components when forecasting diffusion trajectories. SpecKCast, however, targets only temporal redundancy across denoising steps; each computed step still processes the full token grid and therefore retains the spatial redundancy within transformer evaluation. Jointly exploiting temporal and spatial redundancy could enable further acceleration and represents promising direction for future work.
